equipment: Accurate digital scale (0.1 oz / 1 g precision) — all ingredients including lye, water, and oils must be weighed, never measured by volume
Stick blender (immersion blender) dedicated to soap making
Heat-safe, non-aluminum lye-mixing pitcher (heavy-duty polypropylene plastic or stainless steel — lye reacts dangerously with aluminum)
Large stainless steel or heat-safe plastic mixing bowl/pot for oils (never aluminum, tin, or non-stick coatings)
Instant-read or infrared thermometer (two thermometers make tracking lye and oil temps easier)
Silicone spatulas and a heavy-duty plastic or silicone spoon for stirring lye
Soap mold: silicone loaf mold, wood mold lined with freezer paper, or individual cavity molds
Safety gear: chemical-splash goggles, nitrile or rubber gloves, long sleeves, apron, closed-toe shoes
Small containers for pre-weighing lye, fragrance, and colorants
Fine-mesh sieve (for straining lye solution or dispersing additives)
Spray bottle of 99% isopropyl alcohol (optional, to prevent soda ash on the poured soap)
Wire soap cutter or sharp non-serrated knife for cutting bars
Towels or a blanket for insulating the mold, and wax/parchment paper for curing racks
safety: Lye (sodium hydroxide) is highly corrosive. Wear splash goggles, gloves, long sleeves, and closed-toe shoes the entire session, and work with no children, pets, or distractions in the room.
ALWAYS add lye to water — never pour water onto lye. Remember it as 'snow falling on a lake.' Reversing the order can cause a violent, volcano-like eruption of caustic solution.
Only add lye to cool or room-temperature liquid. The solution self-heats to over 200°F within seconds; adding lye to hot liquid makes it boil over.

Mix the lye solution in a well-ventilated spot (open window, outdoors, or a sink you can rinse). Turn your face away and avoid breathing the strong fumes released in the first minute; wear a mask if ventilation is poor.
If lye or raw soap batter touches skin, immediately flush with copious amounts of cool running water. Seek medical attention for eye contact or burns.
Never use aluminum bowls, pots, or utensils — lye reacts with aluminum and releases flammable hydrogen gas. Use stainless steel, heavy-duty plastic, or silicone only.
Label your lye container and lye solution clearly, and set the cooling solution in a safe place out of reach of children and pets — it looks exactly like plain water.
Discard lye that is clumpy or hard: lumps mean moisture contamination, and it will neither weigh nor perform correctly.
Raw soap batter is still caustic for 24-48 hours; wear gloves when pouring, cleaning up, and unmolding fresh soap.
Weigh everything with a digital scale — volume measurements (cups/spoons) are not accurate enough and can leave a bar with dangerous excess lye.

phases.title: Phase 1 — Choose the Recipe and Prepare the Workspace
steps: Run every recipe (even a published one) through a lye calculator before you start, to confirm the sodium hydroxide and water amounts are correct for your exact oils; a 5% superfat is the standard beginner setting.
If formulating your own first recipe, a classic beginner ratio is 34% olive oil, 33% coconut oil, and 33% palm oil.
Clear the kitchen of children, pets, and distractions; open a window for ventilation and set out all equipment so you never leave mid-process.
Put on goggles, gloves, long sleeves, apron, and closed-toe shoes before touching the lye container.
Line a wood mold with freezer paper (silicone molds need no lining) and set it where the filled mold can rest undisturbed for 24-48 hours.

phases.title: Phase 2 — Mix the Lye Solution
steps: Weigh the distilled water into a heat-safe, non-aluminum pitcher and set it in the sink to catch any splashes.
Weigh the sodium hydroxide (lye) into a separate dry container on the digital scale.
Slowly sprinkle the lye into the cool water while stirring with a heavy-duty plastic or silicone spoon; never dump it in all at once and never add the water to the lye.
Keep your face turned away — the solution shoots above 200°F and gives off strong fumes for a minute or so; stir until every granule is dissolved and the cloudy liquid turns clear.

Set the labeled solution in a safe, ventilated spot away from children and pets and let it cool to roughly 90-115°F, which typically takes 30-40 minutes (a few ice cubes counted as part of the water weight can speed this up).

phases.title: Phase 3 — Prepare the Oils
steps: While the lye cools, weigh the solid oils and butters (coconut oil, palm oil, shea, etc.) and melt them gently on the stove or in short microwave bursts.
Weigh the liquid oils (olive, sweet almond, castor, etc.) and stir them into the melted hard oils — adding room-temperature liquid oils also helps bring the temperature down.
Bring the combined oils to roughly 90-110°F; most soapers combine when both lye solution and oils are between 90°F and 110-130°F.
Do not obsess over matching temperatures exactly — oils and lye can be 10-20°F apart with no problem; use an ice-water bath under the oil pot if it needs faster cooling.
Pre-measure your fragrance/essential oil and any colorants or additives now, so they are ready the moment the batter reaches trace.

phases.title: Phase 4 — Combine and Bring to Trace
steps: With safety gear still on, rest the stick blender shaft against the side of the oil pot and pour the cooled lye solution slowly down the shaft to prevent splashing and air bubbles.

Tap the fully submerged stick blender bell on the bottom of the pot to release trapped air, then pulse in short bursts of a few seconds, hand-stirring with the motor off between bursts — running it continuously can burn out the motor and thicken the batter too fast.

Watch for thin (light) trace: the batter turns uniformly opaque with no oil streaks and thickens to a thin cake-batter or warm-custard consistency where drips briefly rest on the surface; this typically takes 2-10 minutes.

If left or blended longer the batter progresses to medium trace (pudding-like, holds soft trailings) and then thick trace (spoonable, holds peaks); pour simple recipes at thin-to-medium trace and work fast once medium trace appears.
Beware false trace: if you soaped cool with lots of hard oils, a thickening that melts back to liquid when warmed is solidifying fat, not true emulsion — keep blending until thickness holds.

phases.title: Phase 5 — Additives and Pour
steps: At light trace, blend or stir in your fragrance or essential oil, colorants, and additives (clays, oatmeal, honey — dilute powders in a little oil or water first to avoid clumps).
Pour the batter into the prepared mold in one steady stream, scraping the pot with a spatula.
Firmly tap the mold on the counter several times to knock out air pockets, then texture or smooth the top with a spatula.
Optionally spritz the surface lightly with 99% isopropyl alcohol every few minutes for the first hour to help prevent soda ash (the harmless white film that can form on top).

phases.title: Phase 6 — Insulate, Gel Phase, and Saponify
steps: Cover the mold with cardboard or its lid and wrap with a towel or blanket if you want to force gel phase, during which the soap self-heats up to about 180°F and takes on a brighter, slightly translucent, shiny look.

Gel phase is purely aesthetic and optional: skip insulation (or refrigerate/freeze the mold for 24 hours) for a matte, pastel, ungelled bar — but avoid a partial gel ring by committing to one approach; milk and honey soaps should NOT be insulated because their sugars overheat.
Leave the mold undisturbed for 24-36 hours while saponification finishes; peek occasionally, and if a crack forms down the center the soap is overheating — uncover it and move it somewhere cooler.
Keep gloves on for any handling during this window; the soap is still mildly caustic until saponification completes.

phases.title: Phase 7 — Unmold, Cut, and Cure
steps: Unmold after 24-48 hours, when the soap is firm and pulls cleanly from the mold; high-coconut/palm recipes release faster, while high-olive (castile-style) recipes can need up to a week — refrigerating a stubborn silicone mold for a few hours helps.
Cut loaf soap into bars soon after unmolding while it is still easy to slice, using a wire cutter or sharp knife.
Stand the bars on wax or parchment paper, spaced apart for airflow, in a dry, dim, room-temperature spot out of direct sunlight.

Cure for a minimum of 4 weeks (4-6 weeks is standard), turning the bars occasionally so all sides dry evenly; curing lets excess water evaporate and the crystal structure develop, giving a harder, milder, longer-lasting bar with better lather.

After curing, store finished bars in a cool, dry place with airflow (e.g., an open basket or cardboard box); avoid sealed plastic for natural CP soap, and expect scent from essential oils to soften over many months.

finishing: Do not use the soap before the cure is complete — it is technically safe a few days after saponification, but a 4-6 week cure produces a noticeably milder, harder, better-lathering bar.
Planing or beveling cured bar edges and wiping any soda ash off with a damp cloth or steamer gives a professional finish.
Store cured bars with space between them in a dry, ventilated, dim location; in use, keep the bar on a draining soap dish so it lasts.
Label bars with the date made and full ingredient list; scent and color mellow over time, and gelled bars stay brighter than ungelled ones.
tips: Always run any recipe through a lye calculator yourself — even printed books contain typos, and every oil swap changes the required lye amount.
Use the stick-blender-shaft pouring trick and short pulse bursts: it prevents lye splashes, minimizes air bubbles, and keeps the batter from racing past the trace stage you want.
Soap at moderate temperatures (roughly 90-110°F, with oils and lye within about 10-20°F of each other) for the most forgiving, slow-moving batter — great for beginners.
Master a plain, unscented, uncolored batch first; fragrance oils can accelerate trace dramatically, so learn how the base recipe behaves before adding variables.
To fight soda ash, spritz the poured surface with 99% isopropyl alcohol, use a modest water discount, or gel the soap — all three reduce the white film.
mistakes: Measuring by volume instead of weight — cups and tablespoons are wildly inaccurate for soap and can produce a lye-heavy, skin-burning bar.
Pouring water into lye (instead of lye into water) or adding lye to warm liquid, causing a caustic boil-over 'volcano'.
Using aluminum bowls, pans, or whisks, which react with lye and release flammable hydrogen gas.
Running the stick blender continuously, which burns out the motor, whips in air bubbles, and rockets the batter to thick trace before you can pour.
Unmolding or cutting too early (crumbly, dented, still-soft soap) or skipping/shortcutting the 4-6 week cure, which leaves a soft, harsh, short-lived bar.
Insulating high-sugar batters (milk or honey soaps), which overheat, crack, or volcano in the mold.

equipment: Crock pot / slow cooker dedicated to soap making, large enough that the raw soap fills it no more than HALF full (soap expands during the cook)
Accurate digital scale (0.1 oz / 1 g precision) — weigh everything, never use measuring cups
Stick blender (immersion blender) for bringing the batter to trace
Heat-safe, non-aluminum lye pitcher (heavy-duty plastic or stainless steel)
Instant-read or infrared thermometer for oils, lye solution, and the cooked batter
Heavy-duty silicone or plastic spatulas and a large spoon for folding and scooping the thick cooked soap
Plastic wrap (to seal under/over the crock pot lid and retain moisture during the cook) plus the pot's own lid
Large whisk for stirring down a rising 'soap volcano'
Heat-tolerant soap mold — silicone or a lined wood/loaf mold that can take soap going in at 160-180°F
Safety gear: chemical-splash goggles, nitrile or rubber gloves, long sleeves, apron, closed-toe shoes
pH strips or a zap-test routine to confirm the cook is complete
Small cups for pre-weighing fragrance, superfat oil, and additives
Wire cutter or sharp knife for slicing, and wax paper for the curing rack
safety: Lye (sodium hydroxide) is highly corrosive: goggles, gloves, and long sleeves are the non-negotiable uniform for the entire session, with kids and pets locked out of the workspace and good ventilation throughout.
ALWAYS pour lye into water, never water into lye — the reverse can react violently and erupt out of the container.
Add lye only to cool liquid (it self-heats past 200°F) and avoid breathing the temporary but strong fumes; mix at arm's length near an open window, in a sink, or outdoors.

Never fill the crock pot more than half full of raw soap, and NEVER leave hot process soap unattended while it cooks — unattended batches can expand into a caustic 'soap volcano' that overflows the pot. Stay in the room, especially the first 30 minutes, and stir a rising batch down with a long whisk.
Do not heat your oils above 180°F, and never add hot lye solution to very hot oils in an already-heated crock pot — the combination can create a scalding, caustic mess.

The cooked batter is 160-180°F when it comes out of the pot: it is a burn hazard even after the lye is neutralized, so never touch it bare-handed — use a spatula or plastic wrap as a barrier when pressing it into the mold.
Use only stainless steel, heavy-duty plastic, or silicone tools — no aluminum anywhere in the process.
If lye or raw batter contacts skin, flush immediately with plenty of cool running water; get medical help for eye exposure.
Keep the labeled cooling lye solution out of reach — it is clear and looks like water.
New to soap? Make a couple of cold process batches first so you can recognize trace and handle lye confidently before adding the cooking stage.

phases.title: Phase 1 — Prepare Recipe, Workspace, and Crock Pot
steps: Run your recipe through a lye calculator (5% superfat is a good default) and confirm the total batch volume will fill the crock pot no more than half full.
Favor recipes with a good share of slow-moving liquid oils (olive, etc.); very high coconut/palm recipes trace and cook extremely fast and are harder to manage in hot process.

Full water (no water discount) is your friend in hot process — extra water keeps the cooked batter fluid enough to mold; many makers also reserve part of the liquid (or add yogurt/milk after the cook) for a smoother finish.
Suit up in goggles, gloves, and long sleeves; clear the room of children, pets, and distractions, and plan to stay with the pot for the entire cook.
Prepare your mold now (line wood molds with freezer paper) — once the cook ends you must work fast, and confirm the mold tolerates soap entering at 160-180°F.

phases.title: Phase 2 — Mix the Lye Solution
steps: Weigh the distilled water into a heat-safe, non-aluminum pitcher set in the sink.
Weigh the sodium hydroxide separately, then slowly sprinkle it into the cool water while stirring, keeping your face turned from the fumes.

Stir until fully dissolved and clear, then set the labeled solution aside to cool for about 15-20 minutes — hot process does not require the lye to cool as far as cold process, but cooler lye lowers the volcano risk.

phases.title: Phase 3 — Melt the Oils in the Crock Pot
steps: Weigh the solid oils and butters directly into the crock pot and melt them on LOW, then stir in the weighed liquid oils.
Bring the oils to roughly 120-150°F — comfortably warm, and never above 180°F.
Cooking on the LOW setting (typical slow cookers run about 165°F on low and near 200°F on high) gives steady heat with far less volcano risk than high.
Pre-measure your fragrance/essential oil, superfat oil (if adding one after the cook), and any additives so they are ready the instant the cook finishes.

phases.title: Phase 4 — Combine and Bring to Trace
steps: Rest the stick blender shaft against the side of the crock pot and slowly pour the lye solution down the shaft into the oils to prevent splashing.
Stir with the blender off to incorporate, then pulse in short bursts, keeping the bell fully submerged and tapping it on the pot bottom occasionally to release air bubbles.

Alternate pulsing and hand-stirring until you reach a solid medium-to-thick trace — the batter should be thick like pudding and hold trailings on the surface (this can take from 2-3 minutes up to 10-15 depending on the recipe).
Scrape the thin film of batter off the pot sides down into the main batter with a spatula so it doesn't crust during the cook.

phases.title: Phase 5 — The Cook
steps: Put the lid on (many soapers stretch plastic wrap under or over the lid to lock in steam — moisture retention is vital) and cook on LOW; resist opening the lid, which lets water escape and stiffens the batter.
Expect the cook to take roughly 30-60 minutes total (about 45 minutes in a typical slow cooker; every model differs). Set a timer and check through the lid every 15 minutes.

Watch the stages of saponification: the cream-colored opaque batter first darkens and turns gelatinous/translucent at the hot edges, then the gel works inward; the batter may puff, rise, or fold over itself like waves — this is normal.
If the soap climbs toward the rim, stir it down with a long whisk — this is why you never walk away, especially in the first 30 minutes.

The batch is done when ALL of the soap — including the center — looks glossy and translucent like petroleum jelly (the 'vaseline stage') with a texture like thick mashed potatoes and no opaque cream-colored pockets remaining; if the middle still looks creamy, keep cooking in 15-minute increments.

phases.title: Phase 6 — Test Doneness, Cool Slightly, and Add Extras
steps: Confirm saponification is complete: a pH strip pressed to a smear of cooled batter should read below about 10, or do a careful 'zap test' — touch a cooled crumb to your tongue; a battery-like zap means unreacted lye and more cook time, no zap means done.
Turn off the crock pot (lift the ceramic insert out onto a potholder) and let the batter cool 10-15 minutes with the lid off before adding anything delicate.
Stir in your superfat oil first if using one (e.g., reserved butter or a luxury oil), since the lye is now consumed it stays as free conditioning oil.

Add fragrance or essential oil once the batter is under about 180°F — added hotter, much of the scent simply vaporizes into the room; sugary additives like honey, milk, or yogurt also scorch and brown if the soap is too hot, so this brief cool-down protects them too.
Stir everything in quickly and thoroughly — the batter thickens fast as it cools, and a stiff batter is hard to mold.

phases.title: Phase 7 — Mold the Soap
steps: Working quickly while the soap is still hot and pliable, spoon or 'plop' the thick batter into the prepared mold in stages.

After each few scoops, firmly tap or rap the mold on the counter to knock out the air pockets that the chunky texture traps (support flexible column/silicone molds with rubber bands or your hands so hot soap can't squeeze out).
Press the soap down and level the top using a spatula or a sheet of plastic wrap over your hand — never bare skin, the soap is around 160-180°F.
Texture the top rustically if you like; hot process is naturally rustic-looking and will not pour glass-smooth like cold process.

phases.title: Phase 8 — Unmold, Cut, and Cure
steps: Let the soap sit in the mold about 24 hours (1-2 days for larger loaves) until fully cool and firm, then unmold.
Slice into bars with a knife or wire cutter soon after unmolding, while the loaf is easiest to cut.
Because saponification finished in the pot, the soap contains no active lye and can technically be used the next day — but it will be soft and short-lived if used immediately.

For best quality, cure the bars on wax paper with airflow for 4-6 weeks (a bare-minimum week for a 'quick' bar): water evaporates, the bar hardens, lather improves, and it lasts far longer in the shower.
Cleanup is easy — soak the crock pot in warm water and the now-saponified residue rinses out as soap.

finishing: Cure hot process bars just like cold process: spaced on wax paper in a dry, airy, dim spot, turned occasionally, for 4-6 weeks even though the soap is already lye-free.
Expect a rustic, slightly textured 'country' look; you can smooth the tops while molding or embrace the texture as the signature of hot process.
Store cured bars in a ventilated, dry place out of sunlight; like all handmade soap they do best on a draining dish in use.
If a finished batch turned out overcooked, dry, and crumbly, it can be rescued: chop it, add about 1 ounce of hot water per pound of soap (an ounce at a time), and reheat gently to rebatch.
tips: The one unbreakable rule: never leave hot process soap cooking unattended — volcanoes happen fast, and every ruined-batch story starts with 'I just stepped out for a minute.'
Seal the crock pot with plastic wrap under a tight lid so you can watch the stages without lifting the lid; retained steam keeps the batter fluid and mold-able.
Cook on LOW: low-and-slow dramatically reduces volcano risk, and slow cookers already hold saponification-friendly temperatures (~165°F on low).
Add fragrance, honey, milk, or yogurt only after a 10-15 minute cool-down below ~180°F — heat is the enemy of scent retention and sugar-based additives.
Since the lye is consumed before extras go in, hot process is ideal for fragile additives and precise superfatting — you control exactly which oil remains unsaponified.
mistakes: Overfilling the crock pot (more than half full) or walking away during the cook, ending in a caustic soap volcano over the counter.
Adding fragrance to soap hotter than ~180°F, so most of the scent evaporates into the room instead of staying in the bars.
Lifting the lid repeatedly or cooking uncovered, which evaporates water and leaves a stiff, dry, impossible-to-mold batter.
Molding too slowly — the batter sets as it cools, trapping large air pockets and leaving crumbly gaps in the finished bars (tap the mold firmly between scoops).
Skipping the doneness test (zap/pH) or the cure: undercooked soap still contains active lye, and uncured bars stay soft and dissolve quickly.
Using a mold that cannot handle 160-180°F soap, which warps thin plastic molds.

equipment: Melt and pour soap base (start with a simple clear or white SFIC-style base; shea, goat milk, aloe, and honey bases come later)
Digital scale to weigh base, fragrance, and colorants
Large microwave-safe glass measuring cup / funnel pitcher with a pour spout, or a double boiler
Dedicated soap-making cutting board and a sharp, non-serrated knife for cubing the base
Heat-safe silicone spatula and a chopstick or spoon for stirring
Instant-read or infrared thermometer — essential for pour and layering temperatures
Spray bottle filled with 99% isopropyl (rubbing) alcohol
Silicone or sturdy plastic soap molds (individual cavities or a loaf mold)
Skin-safe colorants made for melt and pour (liquid dyes, micas, or color blocks) and skin-safe fragrance or essential oils
Pipettes or droppers for measuring fragrance accurately
Fine-mesh sieve for straining diluted powdered colorants
Plastic wrap (cling film) for airtight wrapping of finished bars
Wax paper and paper towels to protect the work surface
safety: No lye handling is required — the base has already been saponified in a factory — which makes melt and pour the safest method and the right one for making soap with kids (with an adult running the melting).
Melted soap base is HOT (120-140°F+) and behaves like hot syrup: it clings to skin, so handle the pitcher with dry hands or a towel and keep young children away from the melting and pouring steps.
Heat in short bursts and never let the base boil — overheated base can scorch, smell burnt, discolor, and become gloppy and unworkable; it can also burn you when stirred.
Use only skin-safe, cosmetic-grade colorants and fragrance/essential oils intended for soap — never candle fragrance, potpourri oil, or craft glitter that is not cosmetic grade.

Follow the supplier's fragrance calculator for your exact fragrance and base; typical melt and pour usage is well under 1 ounce per pound of base, and essential oils should be dosed by percentage (commonly around 0.5-1%).
Isopropyl alcohol is flammable — spray it away from open flames and stove burners.
Work on a protected surface; spilled base hardens quickly but stays slippery, so wipe drips while warm.
If using the microwave, use only microwave-safe glass or plastic and stir between every burst so heat cannot pocket and superheat.

phases.title: Phase 1 — Prepare the Workspace and Mold
steps: Cover the work surface with wax paper, set out the mold on a flat tray or cutting board you can move without flexing it, and pre-measure your colorant and fragrance.
Weigh how much base your mold holds (fill a cavity with water and weigh it as an estimate, or use the mold's stated ounce capacity) so you cut only what you need.
For intricate or detailed molds, spritz the inside of the mold lightly with rubbing alcohol right before filling — the alcohol helps the soap settle into every nook for a crisp impression.

phases.title: Phase 2 — Cut and Melt the Base
steps: Cut the weighed soap base into small, even cubes about 1/2 inch to 1 inch — small uniform pieces melt quickly and evenly without hot spots.

Microwave method: heat the cubes in a microwave-safe pitcher in 30-second bursts, stirring after every burst; as the base is nearly melted, drop to 10-15 second bursts and stop as soon as the last small chunks stir smooth.
Double-boiler method: melt the cubes in a heat-safe container over gently simmering water, stirring occasionally, for more even, scorch-proof heating on larger batches.
Remember the base begins to melt around 120-125°F — full melt only needs the 130-140°F range, so never let it simmer or boil; overheated base turns thick, cloudy, and can smell burnt.
Keep a lid, plate, or plastic wrap loosely over the pitcher between steps to slow evaporation and skin formation.

phases.title: Phase 3 — Color and Fragrance
steps: Let the melted base cool slightly (toward 130-140°F) before adding extras — very hot base burns off fragrance and can distort some colorants.

Stir in colorant a little at a time: liquid dyes and color blocks stir straight in; for powdered micas or natural colorants, first disperse the powder in 2-3 times as much rubbing alcohol (or a splash of liquid glycerin), mix until smooth, strain through a fine sieve if lumpy, then add the slurry in small portions until you reach the shade you want.

Add your skin-safe fragrance or essential oil at the supplier's calculated rate (measure with a pipette on the scale — do not free-pour) and stir gently but thoroughly for 20-30 seconds, avoiding whipping in bubbles.
Work at a deliberate pace: melt and pour cools and skins over quickly, and a skin on the pouring pitcher means it is time for a brief 5-10 second reheat.

phases.title: Phase 4 — Pour and Set
steps: Check the temperature and pour into the mold at roughly 120-130°F (at or below 140°F for a single-color pour) — hot enough to flow smoothly, cool enough not to warp thin plastic molds or sink embeds.
Pour slowly and close to the mold surface in a steady stream to minimize bubbles.
Immediately spritz the surface once or twice with 99% isopropyl alcohol to pop the surface bubbles for a glassy finish.

Leave the mold flat and undisturbed to harden — small cavity bars set in about 1-2 hours, while a full loaf can take 4-12 hours or overnight; moving or flexing the mold early causes cracks and dents (the refrigerator for 10-15 minutes can speed small molds, but never the freezer for long).

phases.title: Phase 5 — Layering (Optional Design Work)
steps: Pour the first layer at or below about 140°F and spritz it with alcohol to pop bubbles, then let it set until it forms a solid skin — test by blowing gently on the surface or tapping the mold side; nothing should ripple.

Keep the next color melted and monitor it with a thermometer: pour each subsequent layer at about 125-130°F — any hotter and it will melt through or break the layer underneath (the base itself starts melting at 120-125°F).
Right before pouring the new layer, spritz the set layer generously once with rubbing alcohol — the alcohol slightly dissolves the surface so the layers fuse and won't split apart when cut.
Pour the new layer slowly over the back of a silicone spatula held just above the surface, so the stream lands softly instead of punching through the skin.

Repeat spritz-set-pour for every layer; weigh the base into equal portions beforehand if you want perfectly even stripes, and be patient — cool-and-firm between layers is what gives razor-straight lines.
Do not overdo the alcohol between layers: a light, even spray bonds them, but soaking the surface can actually make layers separate after cutting.

phases.title: Phase 6 — Unmold, Wrap, and Store
steps: Wait until the soap is completely cool and hard all the way through (several hours for loaves), then flex the mold gently and press from the back to release the bars, or cut a loaf into bars with a sharp knife.
There is NO cure time — melt and pour soap is ready to use as soon as it is cool and hard.

Wrap each bar tightly in plastic wrap (or shrink wrap) as soon as it is unmolded and cool: melt and pour bases are loaded with glycerin, which pulls moisture from the air and forms 'glycerin dew' — sticky beads of sweat — on unwrapped bars, especially in humid climates.
Buff away fingerprints or dust on the shiny surface with a light wipe of rubbing alcohol on a soft cloth before wrapping.
Store wrapped bars in a cool, dry, low-humidity place out of direct sunlight; save every scrap and off-cut in an airtight container — they remelt perfectly for embeds and future batches.

finishing: Wrap bars airtight in plastic wrap immediately after they cool to prevent glycerin dew; add a decorative band or label over the wrap for gifting or sale.
If dew has already formed, set the bars under a fan in a dry room to evaporate the droplets, wipe gently, and then wrap airtight.
Melt and pour bars are ready to use immediately — no cure — but they last longest kept wrapped until use and drained between uses.
Label with ingredients (base manufacturer's INCI list plus your additives), fragrance, and date; well-wrapped bars keep for a year or more.
tips: Temperature is everything: an inexpensive infrared thermometer turns layering from guesswork into a repeatable 125-130°F process.
Spritz rubbing alcohol twice when layering — once right after each pour to pop bubbles, and once right before the next pour so the layers weld together.
Chop the base small and melt low-and-slow in 30-second then 10-second bursts; a base you never scorch stays crystal clear and easy to work.
Dilute powdered colorants in 2-3x their volume of rubbing alcohol and strain before adding, and leave the last speckle-laden dribble of soap in the pitcher for speck-free bars.
Save and remelt every scrap and 'failed' bar — chopped scraps become embeds, confetti soap, or get diluted into fresh base to lighten an over-colored batch.
mistakes: Overheating or boiling the base, which scorches it — burnt smell, yellow cast, gloppy texture — and ruins clarity in clear bases.
Pouring a new layer too hot (above ~130°F) or onto a layer without a firm skin, so it melts through and the colors bleed into each other.
Skipping the alcohol spritz between layers (layers pop apart when the loaf is cut) — or soaking the surface with too much alcohol, which can also cause separation.
Adding fragrance or delicate colorants to base that is far too hot, weakening the scent and shifting the color.
Leaving finished bars unwrapped, so glycerin dew beads all over the surface in humid air.
Using non-cosmetic additives (candle fragrance, craft glitter, crayons) or guessing fragrance amounts instead of using a fragrance calculator.

equipment: Digital kitchen scale (all ingredients measured by weight, not volume, for consistent results)
Two large non-reactive mixing bowls (stainless steel or glass) - one for dry ingredients, one for wet
Fine-mesh sifter or sieve for de-clumping baking soda and citric acid
Small spray bottle with a fine mist, filled with witch hazel
Two-piece bath bomb molds (stainless steel spheres) or silicone/plastic molds
Nitrile or latex gloves (citric acid irritates skin and strips nail polish)
Dust mask and safety glasses for handling powdered citric acid
Whisk and flexible spatula
Drying rack, tray, or folded towel lined with parchment or a soft surface
Shrink wrap bags or airtight containers for finished bombs
safety: Wear gloves for the entire mixing process - prolonged contact with citric acid can irritate skin, and per Bramble Berry it will even remove nail polish.
Wear a dust mask when pouring or sifting citric acid and baking soda; the fine powder is unpleasant and irritating to inhale.
Work in a well-ventilated, LOW-HUMIDITY room. Ambient moisture is the number one cause of failed batches - it prematurely activates the baking soda / citric acid reaction.
Keep all liquids (oils, fragrance, colorant, witch hazel) measured precisely; free water in the mix triggers fizzing before the bomb ever reaches the tub.

Use only skin-safe, bath-safe fragrance or essential oils at supplier-recommended usage rates (typically about 0.5-1% of total weight), and use bath-bomb-approved colorants such as water-soluble La Bomb colorants to avoid staining tubs and skin.
If you add carrier oils, consider adding polysorbate 80 so oil emulsifies into the bathwater instead of pooling and making the tub slippery - a genuine slip-and-fall hazard.
Never use food-grade tools that will return to kitchen duty; dedicate equipment to bath and body making.
Keep finished bombs and raw citric acid away from children and pets.

phases.title: Phase 1 - Measure and prepare the dry base
steps: Weigh 2 parts baking soda to 1 part citric acid by weight - this 2:1 ratio is the industry-standard starting point (for example, Soap Queen's lavender bath bomb recipe uses 32 oz baking soda to 16 oz citric acid; The Nerdy Farm Wife uses 429 g baking soda to 177 g citric acid).

Optionally weigh out fillers and boosters: about 4 oz of extra-fine Epsom salt or fine sea salt per 48 oz of base powder adds minerals and boosts fizz, and cream of tartar at 5-10% of your citric acid weight makes a harder, more polished bomb.
Push the baking soda and citric acid through a sifter, or break up every clump with your gloved fingers - clumps become hard white spots and weak points in the finished bomb.
Whisk all dry ingredients together in the large bowl for a full minute so the citric acid is evenly distributed; uneven mixing gives uneven fizz.

phases.title: Phase 2 - Prepare and add the wet ingredients
steps: In a small separate container, combine your liquid ingredients: about 2 oz of lightweight carrier oil (such as sweet almond, borage, or a melted butter like shea) per 48 oz of dry mix, your essential or fragrance oil (about 0.3 oz per 48 oz batch), and a few drops of bath-safe colorant.
If using a carrier oil, add polysorbate 80 at roughly one-third the oil weight (Soap Queen uses 0.7 oz polysorbate 80 with 2 oz borage oil) so the oil disperses in bathwater instead of floating.
Slowly drizzle the wet mixture into the dry ingredients while whisking constantly, then switch to gloved hands and rub the mixture between your fingers to break up any pockets of oil or color.
Mix until the color is uniform and no streaks remain - streaky color means streaky, unevenly fizzing bombs.

phases.title: Phase 3 - Spritz with witch hazel to reach wet-sand consistency
steps: Do the squeeze test: grab a handful of mixture and squeeze hard. If it holds together like damp sand and keeps its shape, it is ready. If it crumbles apart, it needs moisture.

Hold the witch hazel spray bottle in one hand and spritz 2-3 pumps over the surface while mixing continuously with your other gloved hand - witch hazel is used instead of water because it wets the powder enough to bind, then evaporates cleanly, minimizing premature fizzing.
Repeat in rounds of 2-3 spritzes followed by thorough mixing and another squeeze test. Stop the moment the mixture just barely clumps when squeezed - err on the dry side.
Never dump liquid in all at once and never over-spritz: too much moisture starts the fizzing reaction in the bowl and causes bombs to crack, wart, or expand as they dry.

phases.title: Phase 4 - Pack the molds
steps: Overfill BOTH halves of the two-piece mold with mixture, pressing lightly as you pack - firm enough to compact the bottom of each half, but leave the mixture at the top surface loose.
Press the two overfilled halves together firmly in one straight motion; the loose mixture at the seam is what fuses the halves into one solid sphere.
Do not twist or grind the halves against each other - twisting breaks the bond at the seam and the bomb will split along its equator later.
Wipe away the ring of excess mixture that squeezes out of the seam with your fingers.

Tap the closed mold gently on the work surface a few times, flip it, and tap again, then carefully pull the top half of the mold straight off (a slight gentle twist of the metal cap only, not the bomb, helps release it).
Leave the bomb resting in the bottom half of the mold for about 15 minutes before removing that side, as The Nerdy Farm Wife recommends - this prevents flat spots and crumbled bottoms.

If the halves refuse to stick together, scoop the mixture back into the bowl, add one or two more spritzes of witch hazel, remix, and try again; you may need a spritz or two between every bomb to keep the mixture workable.

phases.title: Phase 5 - Dry, cure, and package
steps: Place unmolded bombs on a folded towel or parchment-lined tray where nothing will touch them, and let them air-dry for 24-48 hours in a dry, cool room away from bathrooms, kitchens, dishwashers, and direct fan airflow.
In a dry climate (or dry winter indoor heat), 24 hours of air drying is usually enough before packaging; check that the bomb feels rock-hard and sounds solid when tapped.

In a humid climate, follow The Nerdy Farm Wife's method: place the fresh bombs in the refrigerator for 30-60 minutes to firm them up, then package promptly - long open-air exposure in humidity makes them wart, expand, and soften.
Run a dehumidifier in the drying room if relative humidity is high; the first 24-48 hours are the critical window when ambient moisture can ruin the batch.
Once fully dry, immediately shrink-wrap each bomb or seal batches in airtight containers so they stop absorbing atmospheric moisture.

finishing: Shrink-wrap individual bombs or store them in airtight jars/bags with a desiccant pack; humidity exposure slowly kills fizz even in a finished bomb.
Store in a cool, dry, dark place - never in a bathroom cabinet.
Use within about 6 months for maximum fizz; bombs remain usable afterward but the reaction weakens as the powders slowly absorb ambient moisture.

For sale in the US, label each bomb or package with the product identity, net weight in both ounces and grams, business name and address, and a full ingredient declaration in descending order of predominance (per FDA cosmetic labeling rules as summarized by Marie Gale).
Add a usage note advising users to rinse the tub afterward if the recipe contains oils or botanicals.
tips: Test one bomb from every batch in a bowl of warm water before gifting or selling - it should fizz vigorously and spin, not sink and dissolve quietly.
Work fast once the mixture is hydrated; it dries out in the bowl, so keep the witch hazel bottle in hand and re-spritz lightly between molding each bomb.
For harder, shinier bombs, add cream of tartar (5-10% of the citric acid weight) or a teaspoon of kaolin clay per pound of mix.
Embed dried botanicals (a pinch of lavender or petals) in one mold half BEFORE packing so they appear on the face of the bomb - but use sparingly, since petals must be fished out of the tub.
Make bath bombs on a dry day whenever possible; experienced makers check the weather forecast because a rainy, humid day measurably increases failure rates.
mistakes: Using too much liquid (or plain water instead of witch hazel), which triggers the fizz reaction early - the bombs crack, grow warts, or expand out of shape while drying.
Skipping the sifting step, leaving citric acid or baking soda clumps that create weak crumbly spots and uneven fizzing.
Twisting the two mold halves together, which shears the bond at the seam so the bomb splits in half when unmolded or dried.
Drying bombs in a humid room or bathroom, or under a fan blowing directly on them - humidity softens and warts them, and direct airflow dries them unevenly and cracks them.
Packing too little mixture or pressing the halves only loosely, producing a soft, powdery bomb that crumbles - the mixture must be packed firmly with loose material only at the seam.

equipment: Digital kitchen scale (formulate by weight so the preservative percentage is accurate)
Large glass or stainless mixing bowl and a sturdy spatula
Small container for pre-mixing liquid ingredients (oil, fragrance, preservative)
Spray bottle of 70% isopropyl alcohol for sanitizing tools, bowls, and jars
Nitrile gloves
Wide-mouth PET plastic jars with tight lids (plastic, not glass, for anything used near a shower or tub)
Pipettes or a 0.01 g scale for measuring preservative accurately
Labels listing ingredients and a use-by date
Optional: small scoop or spatula to include with each jar so users never dip wet fingers
safety: Sanitize every bowl, spatula, and jar with 70% isopropyl alcohol and let air-dry before starting; a scrub is only as clean as the dirtiest tool that touched it.

Even though a sugar or salt scrub contains no water, it lives in the shower and WILL get water splashed into it - per Soap Queen and the School of Natural Skincare, an anhydrous product that contacts water in use either needs a preservative or must be scrupulously kept dry, because introduced water lets bacteria and mold grow.

Choose the right preservative chemistry: an oil-soluble broad-spectrum preservative such as Phenonip (used in the heated/oil portion, effective pH 3-8) or Optiphen (about 1-1.5%) suits oil-based scrubs; water-soluble Liquid Germall Plus (0.5%) suits emulsified scrubs. Never exceed the supplier's maximum usage rate.
Salt scrubs sting and can burn on freshly shaved, broken, or irritated skin - label them for body use and warn against use on the face or damaged skin.
Oily scrubs make tub and shower floors dangerously slippery; add a slip-hazard warning to the label.
Keep fragrance/essential oils within dermal safety limits for wash-off body products (typically 1-3% total, checked against IFRA guidance for the specific oil).
Wear gloves while filling jars so skin flora never enters the product.

phases.title: Phase 1 - Choose your exfoliant: sugar vs salt
steps: Pick sugar for a gentler all-purpose scrub: granulated sugar crystals are smaller and rounder, dissolve quickly in warm water, and per the HSCG formulating guidance shared on Soap Queen, sugar scrubs are noticeably more gentle on skin.

Pick salt for a more aggressive, mineral-rich scrub: salt is coarser and, as Marla Bosworth notes in the Soap Queen formulating post, particularly good for skin prone to ingrown hairs, and for rough spots like feet and elbows.

Match grain size to the body part: fine granulated sugar or fine sea salt for regular body use, brown sugar (the softest) for delicate areas, and coarse salts only for feet - avoid coarse Epsom or dead sea chunks on thin skin.
Never substitute salt into a recipe intended for the face, and remember salt partially dissolves into any liquid over time, so very fine salt scrubs can lose grit in storage.

phases.title: Phase 2 - Formulate the oil-to-exfoliant ratio
steps: Start from a base of roughly 75-85% exfoliant and 15-25% oils by weight for a classic crumbly scrub - Soap Queen's Wildflower Honey Sugar Scrub uses 18 oz sugar with 1.5 oz jojoba oil plus 3 oz potassium cocoate, and you can add oil in small increments if you prefer a wetter, more emollient texture.

Choose mostly lightweight, easy-rinsing oils (jojoba, sweet almond, apricot kernel, fractionated coconut); the Soap Queen formulating guide warns that heavy oils and butters leave a greasy film, so blend any heavy oil (coconut, olive) with lighter ones.

Optionally add a foaming or self-emulsifying agent - potassium cocoate (liquid soap paste) or a solid emulsifier - so the scrub rinses clean instead of leaving an oil slick; this also reduces the tub-slip hazard.
Weigh everything and write the batch formula down as percentages, so the preservative can be dosed correctly and the batch can be reproduced.

phases.title: Phase 3 - Mix the liquid portion
steps: In the small sanitized container, combine the carrier oil(s) and any potassium cocoate or emulsifier, stirring until uniform (the mix may turn cloudy and thicken - that is normal).
Add the fragrance or essential oil (about 0.2 oz per 22 oz batch in the Soap Queen honey scrub, i.e. roughly 1%).

Add the preservative to the liquid portion at its recommended rate (for example Optiphen at 1-1.5%, or Phenonip at up to 1% dissolved into slightly warmed oil) and stir thoroughly - the preservative must be fully dispersed in the liquid before it meets the sugar or salt.
If any ingredient was warmed to melt (butters, Phenonip), let the liquid portion cool to lukewarm before combining, so the sugar does not begin dissolving on contact.

phases.title: Phase 4 - Combine, texture-check, and jar
steps: Pour the sugar or salt into the large sanitized bowl and break up any clumps.

Add the liquid ingredients to the exfoliant and fold with a spatula or gloved hands until every crystal is evenly coated - the finished texture should resemble wet sand that holds together loosely when squeezed.
Adjust texture: add more exfoliant a spoonful at a time if the scrub looks oily and soupy, or drizzle in a little more oil if it is dusty and will not hold together.
Spoon the scrub into sanitized jars, pressing gently to remove air pockets, wipe the rims, and seal immediately.
Label each jar with the full ingredient list in descending order, the net weight in ounces and grams, and a use-by date.

finishing: Store jars sealed in a cool, dark, dry place; heat and steam accelerate both microbial growth and oil rancidity, so a shower shelf is the worst long-term home for a scrub.
Advise users (on the label or an insert) to scoop with a dry spoon or spatula - or decant a single use into a small dish before showering - and to keep shower water from spraying into the open jar.
Shelf life: an unpreserved scrub kept perfectly dry should carry a conservative 3-month use-by date; a properly preserved scrub is typically good for 6-12 months.
The real expiry is also limited by the shortest-dated oil in the recipe - a scrub can never outlive the rancidity date of its oldest oil, so note your oils' best-by dates when labeling.
Discard immediately at any sign of off smell (rancid crayon odor), color change, visible mold, or pooled water in the jar.
tips: Formulate and dose by weight, not cups - preservatives only work at the correct percentage of total batch weight (Humblebee & Me's preservative guidance and calculator are built entirely around weight).
Even 'optional' preservation is cheap insurance: Soap Queen adds Optiphen to sugar scrubs precisely because the first shower use splashes water and germs into the jar.
Add vitamin E (about 0.5%) as an antioxidant to slow oil rancidity - remembering that an antioxidant extends oil life but is NOT a preservative and does nothing against bacteria or mold.
Brown sugar makes the gentlest scrub, white granulated is the workhorse, and turbinado or coarse salt is for feet only - offer a texture range rather than one grit for everything.
Small jars beat big jars: a 4 oz jar gets used up before contamination or rancidity can win, while a 16 oz jar sits in the shower for months collecting water.
mistakes: Skipping the preservative because 'there's no water in it' - the product is used with wet hands in a shower, and introduced water plus sugar is a perfect microbial growth medium (this is the single most repeated warning from Soap Queen, Humblebee & Me, and the School of Natural Skincare).
Letting water pool in the jar (wet fingers, shower spray, steamy bathroom storage), which can turn an unpreserved scrub moldy within days.
Using only heavy oils or butters, which leaves a greasy, hard-to-rinse film on skin and a slippery, dangerous tub.
Adding fragrance or preservative to a hot oil mixture (degrading them) or pouring hot liquid over sugar so it melts into syrup - always combine lukewarm.
Measuring by volume and guessing the preservative amount, which almost always under- or over-doses it; both failure modes are unsafe.

equipment: Digital scale accurate to at least 0.1 g (0.01 g ideal for preservatives)
Digital thermometer (instant-read or infrared)
Immersion (stick) blender - a whisk alone cannot form a stable emulsion
Two heat-proof glass beakers or funnel pitchers (one for the water phase, one for the oil phase)
Large pot or skillet with 2-3 cm of water plus a wire rack or canning ring, to act as a double boiler / water bath
Spray bottle of 70% isopropyl alcohol for sanitizing
Flexible spatulas and pipettes for cool-down ingredients
Disposable piping bag or zip-top bag for filling bottles cleanly
Final packaging: pump, disc-cap, or flip-top bottles preferred over open jars
Stovetop or portable burner, timer, and paper towels
safety: This is the golden rule from every authority (Soap Queen, Humblebee & Me, School of Natural Skincare, Wholesale Supplies Plus): ANY product containing water - lotion, cream, anything with hydrosols, aloe, or milks - MUST contain a broad-spectrum preservative. Unpreserved lotion can grow mold and bacteria within days to weeks, sometimes invisibly.

Anhydrous whipped body butters and balms (100% oils, butters, waxes) do not support microbial growth and do not require a preservative - but add an antioxidant like vitamin E to delay rancidity, and add a preservative anyway if the product will be scooped with wet fingers or stored in a steamy bathroom.
Sanitize the workspace, every tool, and every container with 70% isopropyl alcohol before starting; work with gloves and tied-back hair.
Use distilled or deionized water only - never tap water, which carries minerals and microbes.
Heat-and-hold both phases at 158°F (70°C) for 20 minutes to kill microbes in the raw ingredients and ensure full emulsifier melt.

Respect preservative parameters: Liquid Germall Plus at 0.5% (max - more is not better), Germaben II at 1%, Optiphen at 1.5%, all added in cool-down below about 104-115°F; check each preservative's pH range and incompatibilities (e.g., Optiphen ND conflicts with BTMS-50).
Hot oil and water phases scald - use pot holders, keep beaker handles inward, and never blend hot liquid in an overfilled container.
Label with an ingredient declaration and follow FDA cosmetic labeling rules if the product leaves your house.

phases.title: Phase 1 - Sanitize and weigh the phases
steps: Spray your counter, beakers, spatulas, immersion blender head, and bottles with 70% isopropyl alcohol and let them air-dry.

Write your formula in percentages totaling 100, then convert to grams for your batch size. A proven beginner structure (cross-referencing Wholesale Supplies Plus and Soap Queen): water phase 70-80% (distilled water, plus 2-5% humectant such as glycerin or sodium lactate); oil phase 15-25% (oils and butters 10-20%, emulsifying wax 3-6%, optional stearic acid 2% as thickener); cool-down 2-3% (preservative about 1% and fragrance up to 2%).

A concrete example - WSP's Basic Body Lotion: 64% distilled water, 3% glycerin, 2% sodium lactate, 16% avocado oil, 5% shea butter, 5% emulsifying wax, 2% stearic acid, 2% fragrance, 1% Germaben II. Humblebee & Me's beginner version: 74% distilled water, 5% sodium lactate, 5% Ritamulse SCG, 15% MCT oil, 1% preservative.
Weigh the water phase ingredients into one heat-proof beaker and the oil phase ingredients (including the emulsifying wax - it always goes in the oil phase) into the other.
Weigh out the cool-down ingredients into small cups and set them aside where they will not be knocked over.

phases.title: Phase 2 - Heat and hold both phases (158°F / 70°C for 20 minutes)
steps: Bring 2-3 cm (about 1 inch) of water to a bare simmer in the pot and place both beakers in this water bath on the wire rack.

Heat both phases to 158°F (70°C), checking with the thermometer, and hold them there for a full 20 minutes - this pasteurizes the ingredients and guarantees the emulsifying wax and butters are completely melted.
Stir each phase occasionally with its own clean spatula; the oil phase is ready only when it is fully transparent liquid with no waxy flecks.
Top up the water phase with a splash of extra distilled water if noticeable evaporation occurs during the hold (some makers pre-weigh about 10% extra water to compensate).

Make sure both phases are at the same temperature (within a few degrees of each other, around 158°F) before combining - combining phases at mismatched temperatures is a classic cause of failed, separated emulsions.

phases.title: Phase 3 - Combine and emulsify
steps: Remove both beakers from the water bath and slowly pour the water phase into the oil phase (or oil into water - consistency matters less than temperature) while stirring.

Immediately blend with the immersion blender in short bursts, keeping the head fully submerged to avoid whipping in air; the mixture will quickly turn opaque, milky white - that color change is the emulsion forming.
Blend for 1-2 minutes, rest, then blend again in short bursts every few minutes as the lotion cools; it will visibly thicken as the temperature drops.
Be patient: lotion reaches most of its thickness as it cools, and full final viscosity only after about 24 hours - do not add more emulsifier just because the warm mixture looks thin.

phases.title: Phase 4 - Cool-down additions (below 104-115°F / 40-45°C)
steps: Let the emulsion cool, stirring occasionally, until it is below about 104°F / 40°C (Humblebee & Me's threshold; WSP uses below 115°F / 45°C) - if you have no thermometer, the beaker should feel only slightly warm, like bath water.

Add the preservative at its correct rate (e.g., Liquid Germall Plus 0.5%, Germaben II 1%, or Optiphen 1.5%) and stir or briefly blend until fully incorporated - adding it hotter than its tolerance degrades it and silently leaves the lotion unprotected.
Add fragrance or essential oil (typically up to 1-2% for body products) and any other heat-sensitive extracts or actives.
Keep the entire cool-down phase to 10% or less of the formula - per Humblebee & Me, dumping too much into an already-formed emulsion can destabilize it.
Give one final short blend so everything is uniform.

phases.title: Phase 5 - Bottle, cure, and label
steps: Spoon or pipe the finished lotion into sanitized bottles using a piping bag or zip-top bag with a corner snipped off, filling from the bottom up to avoid air pockets.

Cap immediately; pump, disc-cap, and flip-top bottles are strongly preferred over open jars because every open-jar scoop introduces air and skin flora (if you must use a jar, use the preservative at its maximum recommended rate).
Wipe bottles clean, then let the lotion sit 24 hours to reach final thickness before judging or adjusting the formula.
Label with product identity, net weight in ounces and grams, business name and address, and the full INCI ingredient list in descending order of predominance.
Date each batch and keep a batch log (formula, lot numbers, date) so any problem can be traced.

finishing: Store finished lotion in a cool, dark place away from direct sunlight and heat; heat stresses both the emulsion and the preservative.
A properly preserved lotion in clean packaging is typically good for about 1 year, but never longer than the earliest expiry/rancidity date of the oils used in it.
Watch for spoilage signs at every use: separation, off or sour smell, color change, or any fuzzy growth means discard the whole container immediately - and remember contamination is often invisible.

For anhydrous whipped butters: store below about 75°F so they do not melt and lose their whip, no preservative needed if kept dry, and expect roughly a 6-12 month life driven by the oils' freshness (add 0.5% vitamin E to extend it).
If selling, consider basic challenge/microbial testing (home microbial test kits exist, e.g., from Lotion Crafter) before scaling up a new formula.
tips: Formulate in percentages and weigh everything - it makes batches reproducible, scalable, and lets you dose the preservative correctly every time.
More water = thinner lotion; more oils/butters/e-wax = thicker cream. Adjust texture by moving 2-5% between the water and oil phases rather than rewriting the whole formula.

Match the emulsifier to its documented usage rate: Polawax/e-wax NF at 3-6% of total weight (a common rule of thumb is about 25% of the oil phase), BTMS-50 at 1-15% for a conditioning powder-soft feel, Ritamulse SCG at about 1% per 4-5% of oil (max ~25% oil phase) for a natural-certified option.
Fix a separated batch by reheating both it and a little extra emulsifier gently to about 130°F and re-blending - hotter than that risks degrading the preservative already in it.
Germall Plus is the closest thing to a foolproof beginner preservative: broad pH range, water-soluble, hard to deactivate, used at just 0.5%.
mistakes: Skipping the preservative or substituting a non-preservative (vitamin E, grapefruit seed extract, 'natural antibacterials') in a water-containing product - antioxidants slow rancidity but do nothing against bacteria and mold, and unpreserved lotion can be growing pathogens within weeks even while it still looks fine.
Skipping heat-and-hold or combining phases at very different temperatures, which produces an emulsion that splits hours or days later.
Adding preservative or fragrance while the emulsion is still hot (above roughly 104-115°F), which degrades them - the lotion smells weak and, worse, is no longer reliably preserved.
Using tap water, unsanitized tools, or double-dipped fingers, seeding the product with microbes the preservative then has to fight from day one.
Judging thickness too early and over-correcting with extra emulsifying wax - lotion thickens dramatically as it cools over 24 hours, and overloaded e-wax gives a heavy, soapy, draggy skin feel.

equipment: Accurate digital kitchen scale that weighs in grams (all soap ingredients must be weighed, never measured by volume)
Heatproof, lye-safe pitcher for the lye solution (sturdy polypropylene/HDPE plastic or stainless steel; never aluminum, which reacts violently with lye)
Large stainless steel or heatproof plastic mixing bowl or pot for the oils
Stick (immersion) blender reserved for soapmaking only
Digital or infrared thermometer for checking lye-solution and oil temperatures
Silicone loaf mold or individual cavity molds (or a wooden mold lined with freezer paper)
Chemical-splash safety goggles and long chemical-resistant gloves
Long-sleeved clothing, closed shoes, and an apron
Silicone spatulas and stainless spoons dedicated to soapmaking
4-quart crock pot (slow cooker) if using the hot-process option
Old towel or blanket for insulating cold-process soap in the mold
safety: Sodium hydroxide (lye) is caustic and can cause severe chemical burns: always wear goggles, gloves, and long sleeves from the moment you open the lye container until cleanup is finished.
Always sprinkle the lye INTO the water while stirring, never pour water into dry lye, which can cause a violent, eruptive reaction.
Do not breathe the strong fumes released for the first minute or so after lye meets water; mix in a well-ventilated area or near an open window and turn your face away.
Keep children, pets, and any distractions completely out of the workspace while lye or raw soap batter is out (Soap Queen's rule: kids, pets, and tripping hazards out of the soaping space).
Raw soap batter is still caustic until saponification completes; treat splashes on skin by rinsing with copious cool running water.
Any herbal tea used in place of distilled water must be fully chilled before adding lye, or the solution can overheat and volcano.
Rosemary essential oil should be avoided or used only under professional guidance if you are pregnant or have hypertension or epilepsy; substitute lavender.
Keep total essential-oil usage around 2-3% of the oil weight (about 20 g of essential oil per 770 g of base oils in The Nerdy Farm Wife's recipe), and never use undiluted essential oils on skin.
Label the lye container clearly and store it sealed, dry, and out of reach of children.

phases.title: Phase 1 - Set up the workspace and a benchmark recipe
steps: Suit up in goggles, gloves, long sleeves, and closed shoes before touching any ingredient.
Clear a ventilated work area, cover surfaces, and confirm children and pets are out of the room.

Use a proven, lye-calculated shampoo-bar recipe; The Nerdy Farm Wife's benchmark is 283 g olive oil, 227 g coconut oil, 113 g castor oil, 113 g sunflower or sweet almond oil, 57 g jojoba oil, 108 g sodium hydroxide, and 283 g distilled water for hot process (reduce to 255 g water for cold process), scented with 15 g peppermint and 5 g rosemary essential oil.

Note that shampoo bars differ from body soap mainly through a high castor-oil percentage for a dense, bubbly lather, and generous superfat; Lovely Greens' Herbal Academy recipe runs a 16% superfat with a 25% lye-solution concentration.
If you have never made soap, read a full cold-process primer (for example The Nerdy Farm Wife's Soap Making 101) before you begin, and run every recipe change through a lye calculator.

phases.title: Phase 2 - Make the lye solution
steps: Weigh the distilled water (or fully chilled herbal tea) into your heatproof lye-safe pitcher.
Weigh the sodium hydroxide separately, then slowly sprinkle and stir the lye into the water - never the reverse.
Stir gently until the solution turns clear, keeping your face away from the temporary fumes.
Set the solution somewhere safe to cool: about 30-40 minutes for cold process so it drops to 100-110 F (38-43 C), or only 15-20 minutes if you are making hot-process soap in a crock pot.

phases.title: Phase 3 - Prepare the oils
steps: Weigh the solid oils (coconut oil, and palm if your recipe uses it) and melt them gently on the stove or in short microwave bursts.
Weigh and stir in the liquid oils (olive, castor, sunflower or almond, jojoba).
Warm the combined oils, if needed, to roughly 90-100 F (32-38 C); Soap Queen aims to have oils and lye each around 100 F when combined.

phases.title: Phase 4 - Combine and bring to trace
steps: Pour the cooled lye solution slowly into the oils, pouring down the shaft of the stick blender to minimize splashes.
Alternate short bursts of the stick blender with hand stirring; trace usually takes two to eight minutes.
Stop when the batter reaches 'trace' - it is uniformly emulsified and a drizzle from the spatula leaves a faint trail on the surface.

If your recipe adds a citric-acid/panthenol solution to lower the final pH (Soap Queen dissolves 0.5 oz citric acid and 0.3 oz DL-panthenol in 4 tablespoons distilled water), blend it in at light trace.

phases.title: Phase 5 - Cold-process option: mold and insulate
steps: Stir the essential oils into the batter at trace.
Pour the batter into the prepared mold, tap the mold to release air bubbles, then cover and insulate it with a towel or blanket.
Leave the soap in the mold for 1 to 2 days until firm enough to release cleanly.
Unmold and slice into bars with a sharp knife or soap cutter while still slightly soft.

phases.title: Phase 6 - Hot-process option: crock pot cook
steps: Transfer the traced batter to a crock pot set to low and cover it.
Cook for 1 hour, stirring every 15 minutes, as the soap moves through gel phase to a mashed-potato/applesauce texture.
Let the cooked soap cool a few minutes, stir in the essential oils, then quickly spoon the thick paste into the mold, pressing out air pockets.
Keep the soap in the mold for 24 hours before unmolding and cutting.

phases.title: Phase 7 - Cure
steps: Stand the cut bars on a rack or paper-lined tray with air space between them, out of direct sun.
Cure cold-process shampoo bars at least 4 weeks, turning occasionally; high-liquid-oil shampoo recipes benefit from even longer cures (Soap Queen notes they take longer than regular cold process).
Hot-process bars are technically usable right away but still improve with 2 to 3 weeks of cure for hardness and mildness.

finishing: Cure completed bars 4+ weeks (cold process) or 2-3 weeks (hot process) before use, then store them in a cool, dry, airy spot; properly cured soap keeps about a year.
Between uses, keep bars on a draining soap dish so they dry fully and last longer.

Because soap-based shampoo is alkaline (pH around 7-9) while hair prefers acidic, follow each wash with an acidic rinse: Lovely Greens recommends 1 teaspoon apple cider vinegar in 1 cup of water poured through the hair; Soap Queen suggests a mint-ACV rinse.
Label bars with the made-on date and ingredients, and expect a transition period of a week or two as hair adjusts.
Wash all lye-contact equipment carefully in hot soapy water while still wearing gloves; residual raw batter is caustic for 24-48 hours.
tips: Push castor oil to 10-15% of the oil blend - it is the classic shampoo-bar ingredient for dense, conditioning lather.
Use a generous superfat (Lovely Greens' recipe runs 16%) so the bar is gentler on hair than ordinary body soap.
Swap the water for a light, fully chilled herbal tea such as rosemary or nettle for extra hair benefits, keeping the infusion pale so it does not discolor the soap.
Adding a dissolved citric-acid solution at trace (Soap Queen's method) lowers the finished bar's pH and makes it noticeably gentler on hair.

Soap-based shampoo bars suit some hair types but not all; if hair turns gummy or straw-like, an ACV rinse and a conditioner afterward make the biggest difference, and hard-water households may do better with a syndet bar.
mistakes: Pouring water into lye instead of lye into water - this can cause a dangerous eruptive boil-over.
Measuring by volume instead of weight, or skipping the lye calculator after substituting oils, which yields lye-heavy or mushy soap.
Combining lye and oils while too hot (well above 110 F), causing acceleration, cracking, or a soap volcano - especially with milk or honey additives.
Cutting the cure short: an uncured, high-liquid-oil shampoo bar is soft, harsh, and dissolves quickly in the shower.
Using aluminum bowls, whisks, or molds anywhere in the process; lye reacts with aluminum and produces flammable hydrogen gas.

equipment: Accurate digital scale that reads to 0.1 g (surfactant and preservative amounts are small and must be precise)
Small saucepan for a water bath, filled with about 3 cm (1 inch) of water
Heat-resistant glass measuring cups (one for the surfactant phase, one for the oil phase)
Fine-particle dust mask or respirator for handling powdered surfactants
Sturdy silicone spatula and a fork or sturdy spoon for mashing the thick paste
Silicone mold, round bath-bomb mold, or a manual bar press for shaping
Nitrile gloves for kneading and pressing the warm dough
pH strips (optional but useful to confirm the finished bar is roughly pH 5-6, hair-friendly)
Parchment paper and a drying rack for the hardening period
safety: Wear a dust mask whenever you handle powdered or noodle surfactants such as SCI or SLSa - airborne surfactant dust is very irritating to the lungs (Humblebee & Me instructs putting the mask on before weighing).
Work in a ventilated space and avoid stirring powders vigorously while dry.
A broad-spectrum preservative is required because the bar lives in a wet shower environment: Humblebee & Me uses 0.5% Liquid Germall Plus in both the Snowflake and Mango Mango bars.
Liquid Germall Plus is heat-sensitive, so only add it once the mixture has cooled below 50 C (122 F).
Respect supplier maximum-usage rates for fragrance or essential oils in rinse-off hair products (about 1% fragrance in the Mango Mango bar); never exceed IFRA limits.
The melted surfactant paste is very hot after an hour over a water bath - handle the glass cup with a dry towel and let the mash cool until comfortable to touch before hand-shaping.
These bars are pH-balanced and lye-free, which is exactly why they should NOT be confused with soap: do not add lye, and do not sell them as 'soap'.

phases.title: Phase 1 - Formula and prep
steps: Work from a balanced syndet formula: Humblebee & Me's Snowflake Shampoo Bar (about 100 g) uses 30 g Sodium Cocoyl Isethionate (SCI), 25 g Sodium Coco Sulfate, and 20 g Cocamidopropyl Betaine as the surfactant core, with 10 g tucuma (or other) butter, 8 g BTMS-50, 3.5 g cetyl alcohol, 2 g stearic acid, and 0.5 g Liquid Germall Plus.

As a rule of thumb, solid surfactants make up roughly 60-75% of a syndet bar, hardening fats/waxes (BTMS-50, cetyl alcohol, stearic acid, butter) 20-30%, and the cool-down phase (fragrance, preservative, extras) the remainder.
Put on your dust mask before opening any surfactant container, then weigh every ingredient with a 0.1 g scale.
Bring about 3 cm (1 inch) of water to a bare simmer over low to medium-low heat in a small saucepan - this gentle water bath is your only heat source.

phases.title: Phase 2 - Melt the surfactant phase
steps: Weigh the SCI and Cocamidopropyl Betaine into a small heat-resistant glass measuring cup.
Set the cup in the simmering water bath and let it melt slowly; Humblebee & Me reports this typically takes up to an hour.

Stir occasionally and stop when you have a smooth, uniform white paste with no gritty SCI granules remaining - SCI alone melts poorly, which is why it is always melted together with the liquid betaine.

phases.title: Phase 3 - Melt the oil / conditioning phase
steps: Weigh the butter, BTMS-50, stearic acid, and cetyl alcohol into a second heat-resistant glass measuring cup.
Place that cup in the same water bath and melt everything through completely; BTMS-50 and cetyl alcohol are fully fluid by about 70-75 C, so a barely simmering bath is plenty.
Remove both cups from the heat once each phase is uniform and liquid/paste-smooth.

phases.title: Phase 4 - Combine, mash, and cool
steps: Pour the melted oil phase into the surfactant paste and mash and fold everything together with a fork or spatula until it forms one uniform, dough-like mass (Humblebee & Me calls this the 'surfactant mash').
Keep working the mash until it cools; by the time it is evenly combined it should be below 50 C (122 F) - if it still feels hot to the touch, wait before continuing.

Once cool to the touch, add the fragrance or essential oil (about 1% for rinse-off hair products) and the 0.5% broad-spectrum preservative, and knead them in thoroughly so they are evenly distributed.

phases.title: Phase 5 - Press and mold
steps: While the dough is still warm and pliable, firmly press it into a silicone cavity mold, packing in small amounts at a time to eliminate air pockets, or shape it by hand into a puck wearing gloves.

For a professional finish, use a manual bar press or smoosh the dough between the two halves of a bath-bomb mold under strong, even pressure; Humblebee & Me notes bars can be hand-shaped, smooshed into a cavity mould, or pressed with a hand press or powered press.
Unmold gently as soon as the bar is cool and firm enough to hold its shape.

phases.title: Phase 6 - Harden and dry
steps: Set the bars on parchment or a rack in a cool, dry spot with air circulation.
Let them harden and dry for at least 24-48 hours before first use; Humblebee & Me's pressed Creamy French bars rest 3 to 4 days for best hardness and longevity.
The bar is ready when it feels hard and dry all over and no longer dents under firm thumb pressure.

finishing: Store finished bars in a cool, dry place; between showers keep the bar on a draining dish or ledge out of the water stream so it dries fully.
Properly preserved syndet bars typically keep 12 months or more - the limiting factor is usually the shelf life of the softest oil in the formula.
To use, swipe the bar directly over wet hair 3-4 times or lather in hands, massage into the scalp, and rinse; no vinegar rinse is needed because the bar is already pH-balanced.
Wrap gift or sale bars in wax paper or store them in tins only after they are fully dry, and label with ingredients (INCI names) and the preservative used.
Wipe equipment clean while warm - hardened surfactant paste is tedious to remove once cooled.
tips: SCI ('baby foam') is the gentlest workhorse solid surfactant - pairing it with liquid Cocamidopropyl Betaine both mellows the blend further and makes melting possible.
BTMS-50 in a shampoo bar (about 8% in the Snowflake bar) does double duty as hardener and conditioning agent, leaving hair combable straight out of the shower.
If the mash cools and stiffens before you finish molding, return it to the water bath for a minute or two to re-soften - it is very forgiving.
Weigh preservative and fragrance to 0.1 g accuracy; at 0.5% and 1% of a 100 g batch, kitchen-teaspoon guessing ruins the formula.
A syndet bar is the right recommendation for hard-water areas and color-treated hair, where lye-soap shampoo bars leave scum and lift the cuticle.
mistakes: Skipping the dust mask when weighing powdered SCI or SLSa - inhaled surfactant dust causes coughing fits and lung irritation.
Trying to melt SCI on its own or over direct heat: it scorches instead of melting; always combine it with the liquid surfactant over a gentle water bath.
Adding Liquid Germall Plus or fragrance while the mash is above 50 C, which degrades the preservative and flashes off the scent.
Skipping the preservative entirely 'because it is natural' - a bar that sits in a humid shower will grow mold and bacteria without one.
Using the bar (or packaging it) before the 24-48 hour hardening period, which produces a soft bar that dissolves in a week.

equipment: Digital scale accurate to 0.1 g (conditioner-bar preservative and fragrance amounts are tiny)
Small saucepan with about 3 cm (1 inch) of water for a gentle water bath, or a double boiler
Heat-resistant glass measuring cup for melting the heated phase
Silicone spatula for stirring and scraping
Silicone cavity molds (muffin, honeycomb, or bar shapes; a 50 mL cavity makes one full-size bar, 12-15 g cavities make travel minis)
Refrigerator or freezer space for setting the poured bars
Thermometer to confirm the mixture is below 50 C before cool-down additions
70% isopropyl alcohol in a spray bottle to sanitize tools, molds, and work surface
safety: Conditioner bars are anhydrous but live in a wet shower, so include a broad-spectrum preservative (for example 0.5% Liquid Germall Plus, or about 1% Phenoxyethanol-based preservative as in the Wholesale Supplies Plus recipe) at its recommended usage rate.
Add heat-sensitive preservatives and fragrance only after removing the melted phase from heat, once it is below about 50 C (122 F).

Keep fragrance and essential-oil levels within supplier/IFRA maximums for leave-on products; after irritation reports, Humblebee & Me now recommends only 0.1-0.2% fragrance in this kind of bar and warns against spicy essential-oil blends (cinnamon, clove, nutmeg) on skin and scalp.
BTMS-50 is a cationic conditioning emulsifier and is NOT interchangeable with regular (nonionic) emulsifying wax - substituting e-wax removes the conditioning effect entirely.
Melted butters and waxes are hot oil: handle the glass cup with a dry cloth and pour carefully.
Sanitize molds, cups, and spatulas with isopropyl alcohol before starting, since the finished product touches hair and scalp repeatedly.

phases.title: Phase 1 - Understand the formula
steps: Build the bar around BTMS-50, the cationic (positively charged) conditioning emulsifier that bonds to negatively charged hair; anything with 1-2% BTMS-50 is conditioning, and solid bars use far more.

Use a proven ratio: Humblebee & Me's Vanilla Spice Conditioner Bar is 40% BTMS-50 (20 g in a 50 g bar) plus 20% cetyl alcohol (10 g) with nourishing oils making up most of the rest; the Wholesale Supplies Plus bar runs about 27% BTMS-50 with cetyl alcohol, cocoa butter, shea butter, and coconut oil; Humblebee's simpler Cocoa Coconut bars pair BTMS-50 with 47% cocoa butter plus coconut oil.
Plan roughly: 25-40% BTMS-50, 5-20% cetyl alcohol for glide and hardness, 30-50% butters and oils, 1% or less fragrance, plus preservative and optional panthenol or hydrolyzed protein.
Weigh every ingredient on a 0.1 g scale before turning on any heat.

phases.title: Phase 2 - Melt the heated phase
steps: Bring about 3 cm (1 inch) of water to a bare simmer over low to medium-low heat in a small saucepan.
Weigh the BTMS-50, cetyl alcohol, butters, and liquid oils into a heat-resistant glass measuring cup.
Place the measuring cup in the water bath and let everything melt through completely, stirring now and then, until the mixture is fully liquid and uniform (BTMS-50 pellets are the last to disappear).

phases.title: Phase 3 - Cool-down additions
steps: Remove the cup from the heat and stir for a minute so the mixture drops below 50 C (122 F).
Quickly stir in the preservative (e.g., 0.5% Liquid Germall Plus) and the fragrance or essential oil at or below its leave-on maximum (0.1-0.2% is enough to scent the bar).
Stir thoroughly but briefly - the mixture starts to thicken as it cools, and you want it still pourable.

phases.title: Phase 4 - Pour and set
steps: Pour the liquid conditioner into silicone molds: one 50 mL (1.7 fl oz) cavity for a full bar, or 12-15 g cavities for minis (Humblebee fills 15 g honeycomb cavities to only 12 g to avoid sloshing on the way to the fridge).
Transfer the filled mold carefully to the refrigerator and leave the bars to solidify fully (roughly 30-60 minutes for small bars; the freezer speeds this up).
Unmold by flexing the silicone gently once the bars are completely cold and hard.

phases.title: Phase 5 - Rest, test, and use
steps: The bars are usable as soon as they reach room temperature - Humblebee & Me found no meaningful difference after longer rests (weight loss was only 0.4% after 8+ days), so no cure is required.
To use, swipe the bar down the lengths and ends of clean, wet hair a few times, work through with fingers or a wide comb, then rinse; focus on mid-lengths and ends, not the scalp.
Patch-test the finished bar on the inner forearm before first full use, especially if it contains essential oils.

finishing: Let bars dry between uses on a draining soap dish outside the water stream; a conditioner bar that sits in a puddle turns to mush.
Store spares in a cool, dry place away from direct sun; a well-preserved bar keeps about 12 months (limited by the shelf life of its softest oil).
One 50 g bar replaces roughly a bottle of conditioner and can last a single user for months to a year of normal use.
For travel or gifting, store the fully hardened bar in a small tin with a paper liner, and label ingredients with INCI names.
If bars soften in a hot climate, keep them refrigerated or reformulate with more cetyl alcohol/stearic-hard butter - cocoa butter alone melts around 34 C (93 F), below the ~40 C of a hot shower.
